Forty minutes of nodding, then a whispered question in the hallway. I think about that moment a lot.

The person who asked me wasn't slow. They were doing what almost everyone in that room had learned to do: protect the appearance of competence. Asking would have cost them something. So they paid a different price instead.

I wrote a whole chapter about this. It's called Knowledge Hoarding, and it is the quietest of the five forces that shut adult curiosity down.

What's the term everyone at your company uses that you have never actually looked up? No judgement here. I'll start: it took me two years in hospitality to admit I had no idea what RevPAR meant.

posts.title: 107 questions an hour
posts.caption:
107 questions an hour. That's what researchers counted when they recorded young children in 2007.

Then think about your last Tuesday. How many real questions did you ask? Not clarifying questions in a meeting. Real ones. The kind where you actually don't know the answer and you say so out loud.

Nobody outgrows curiosity. A molecular biologist named John Medina puts it bluntly: it isn't possible to outgrow curiosity in the seven or eight decades we spend here. So the problem isn't your brain. It's the rooms you spend your days in.

Count your questions tomorrow. Just count them. That number tells you more about your next five years than your CV does.

posts.title: $300 billion to over $3 trillion
posts.caption:
Microsoft in 2014 was profitable and dying at the same time. That combination is the most dangerous state a company or a career can be in, because nothing looks broken.

What changed wasn't talent. It was permission. Nadella replaced know-it-all with learn-it-all and started meetings by asking what people had learned instead of what they had shipped.

I keep coming back to this case because the comfort zone is the only trap you build out of your own success. Every year of expertise raises the social cost of saying "I don't know." Until one day you're the most competent person in the room and the least curious.

What did you learn last week? Not achieve. Learn.
